title: Property-based testing
description: Property-based testing asserts invariants over generated inputs instead of examples: 'reverse(reverse(x)) == x' for hundreds of random lists. The framework generates inputs, shrinks failures to minimal cases, and finds the edge cases humans forget. It inverts the testing mindset — from 'does it work on my examples' to 'what breaks the invariant'.
mechanism: Define strategies (generators) per type; assert properties; the runner generates N cases, shrinks failures by minimizing the input. Stateful testing extends it to sequences of operations.
algo: O(cases * test). Shrinking is a search over smaller inputs — usually logarithmic-ish.

title: Fuzzing
description: Fuzzing throws random and mutated inputs at code to find crashes, hangs, and assertion failures: coverage-guided fuzzers (AFL++, libFuzzer) mutate the inputs that discover new code paths, evolving toward deep bugs. It found thousands of CVEs in parsers and decoders. The recipe is simple — harness + corpus + time — and the bugs it finds are the ones tests never thought to write.
mechanism: Corpus of seed inputs; mutate (bit flips, splices); run with coverage instrumentation; keep inputs that hit new paths; report crashes with minimized reproducers. Sanitizers (ASan, UBSan) turn silent corruption into loud failures.
algo: O(executions); coverage guidance makes it far better than blind random. Time-bounded: more time, deeper bugs.

title: Mutation testing
description: Mutation testing judges the test suite, not the code: inject small faults (mutants) — flip a comparison, delete a line — and check the suite kills them. Surviving mutants are holes in the tests. The mutation score (% killed) is the honest coverage number; line coverage lies, mutation score does not. It is expensive (mutants x suite), so production use samples mutants and runs incrementally.
mechanism: Generate mutants per mutation operator; run the suite per mutant (or per batch); killed = suite fails. Score = killed/total. Equivalent mutants (same behavior) are the noise — detected by hand or by smarter operators.
algo: O(mutants * suite) naive; sampling + incremental + parallel bring it to practical.

title: The oracle problem
description: Tests need oracles — a way to know the right answer. The oracle problem is that for many programs the right answer is exactly what is hard to compute: the test would reimplement the code. Solutions: metamorphic relations ('sorting twice = sorting once'), differential oracles (two implementations agree), and partial oracles (check properties, not exact values). Naming the oracle strategy is the first step of every test design.
mechanism: Metamorphic: relations over outputs (f(f(x)) == f(x)). Differential: N versions agree. Partial: invariants, not values. Human oracle: golden files reviewed once, then regression.
algo: O(tests); the oracle is the design work, not the execution.
demo:
# metamorphic oracle: no need to know the right answer, only the relation
import random
random.seed(4)

def sort(xs):
    return sorted(xs)

ok = True
for _ in range(200):
    xs = [random.randint(0, 99) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 10))]
    # metamorphic relations: idempotent, permutation-invariant, sorted output
    ok &= sort(sort(xs)) == sort(xs)
    ok &= sort(xs) == sort(list(reversed(xs)))
    ok &= all(a <= b for a, b in zip(sort(xs), sort(xs)[1:]))
print('200 cases x 3 metamorphic relations:', 'all hold' if ok else 'VIOLATION')
print('oracle without knowing answers: relations over outputs')

title: Coverage-guided generation
description: Coverage-guided test generation aims new tests at uncovered code: instrument, find uncovered branches, and solve or search for inputs reaching them. Symbolic execution (KLEE) solves path constraints; search-based (EvoSuite) evolves inputs toward coverage. The result complements human tests — machines cover the branches humans forgot, humans cover the behaviors machines cannot judge.
mechanism: Instrument for branch coverage; worklist of uncovered branches; generate inputs via constraint solving or evolutionary search; add passing ones to the suite. Stop at coverage plateau or time budget.
algo: O(time budget); coverage climbs fast then plateaus — the last 10% is disproportionately expensive.

title: LLM test generation
description: LLMs write plausible tests fast — Arrange/Act/Assert shaped, covering the obvious cases — but they assert what the code does, not what it should do, and they hallucinate APIs. The working pattern: LLM drafts, mutation testing judges (do the tests kill mutants?), humans fix the oracles. Generated tests are a starting draft, never a finished suite.
mechanism: Prompt with the function + context; generate tests; run them; mutation-score the result; human reviews oracles and edge cases. Regenerate on code change (or mark stale).
algo: O(tokens) generation; O(mutants) judging. The oracle review is human.
demo:
# LLM-drafted tests: plausible, but the ORACLE needs human review
def total(xs):
    s = 0
    for x in xs:
        s += x
    return s

# 'LLM draft' (simulated): covers obvious cases...
drafted = [
    ('empty', [], 0),
    ('positive', [1, 2, 3], 6),
]
# ...but misses: negatives, floats, huge lists, non-numbers (no oracle judgment)
missing = ['negatives', 'float precision', 'empty vs None', 'non-numeric input']
passed = all(total(xs) == want for _, xs, want in drafted)
print('drafted tests pass:', passed)
print('draft MISSES (no oracle judgment):', missing)
print('mutation-score the draft; humans fix the oracles')

title: Boundary analysis
description: Bugs cluster at boundaries: 0, 1, -1, max-int, empty, null, off-by-one. Boundary analysis systematically tests the edges of each input domain — min, min+1, nominal, max-1, max — instead of hoping random testing stumbles onto them. It is the cheapest high-yield technique in testing: five cases per boundary, and the bugs it finds are the production incidents.
mechanism: For each input: identify domain boundaries (0, empty, limits, type edges); generate boundary +- 1 cases; assert. Combine with equivalence partitioning (one case per partition, boundaries per edge).
algo: O(boundaries) cases — tiny suites, huge yield.
demo:
# boundaries of: discount applies when p > 100
def discount(p):
    return p * 0.9 if p > 100 else p

cases = [99, 100, 101, 0, -1, 10**18]  # max-1, max, max+1, zero, negative, huge
print(' p        : result (boundary analysis)')
for p in cases:
    print('%10d : %s' % (p, discount(p)))
print('the bug is always at 100 vs 101: test the edge, not the middle')

title: Test doubles
description: Test doubles isolate the unit under test: dummies (pass-through), stubs (canned answers), spies (record calls), mocks (verify interactions), fakes (working implementations, e.g., in-memory DB). The rule is mock roles, not objects — verify the interaction at the boundary, not the internals. Over-mocked tests assert the mock, not the code; they pass while the system breaks.
mechanism: Dependency injection makes doubles possible; the double implements the same interface. Verify state (fakes/stubs) over interactions (mocks) where possible — interaction tests are brittle.
algo: Design pattern; the cost is maintenance of the doubles.
demo:
from unittest.mock import MagicMock

# spy: record how the unit uses its collaborator
mailer = MagicMock()

def checkout(cart, mail):
    total = sum(cart)
    mail.send('user@x.com', 'receipt: %d' % total)
    return total

assert checkout([10, 20], mailer) == 30
mailer.send.assert_called_once_with('user@x.com', 'receipt: 30')
print('spy verified the interaction: to, subject correct')
print('rule: prefer fakes (in-memory DB) over mocks; mock roles, not objects')

title: Snapshot testing
description: Snapshot tests capture output once (human-reviewed) and assert future runs match byte-for-byte: perfect for serializers, renderers, and CLI output where the 'right answer' is 'looks like last time'. The failure mode is blind updating — --update-snapshot without reviewing turns the test into a change detector that approves everything. Review snapshot diffs like code diffs.
mechanism: First run: write snapshot (reviewed). Later runs: compare; diff on mismatch. Update explicitly with review. Store snapshots in version control next to the tests.
algo: O(output) compare. The discipline is reviewing updates.
demo:
import json, hashlib

def render(user):
    return json.dumps({'name': user['name'], 'plan': user['plan']}, sort_keys=True)

SNAPSHOT = '{"name": "Ada", "plan": "pro"}'  # reviewed once, committed
out = render({'name': 'Ada', 'plan': 'pro'})
print('match:', out == SNAPSHOT)
# a change:
out2 = render({'name': 'Ada', 'plan': 'team'})
print('after change, match:', out2 == SNAPSHOT, '-> review the diff before --update-snapshot')
print('blind updating approves everything: review snapshot diffs like code')

title: Parameterized tests
description: Parameterized tests run the same logic over a table of (input, expected) pairs — one test function, dozens of cases, each reported separately. They replace copy-pasted test methods and make the case list the documentation. The table is data: add a case by adding a row, and the edge cases accumulate where everyone can see them.
mechanism: Decorator/table-driven: for each row, run and report independently. Name each case; failures point at the row, not the function.
algo: O(rows) cases; the table is the spec.
demo:
# table-driven: the case list IS the documentation
cases = [
    ('empty', [], 0),
    ('single', [7], 7),
    ('mixed', [-1, 2, -3, 4], 2),
    ('floats', [0.1, 0.2], 0.30000000000000004),
]

def total(xs):
    s = 0
    for x in xs:
        s += x
    return s

failed = 0
for name, xs, want in cases:
    ok = total(xs) == want
    failed += not ok
    print('%-8s %s' % (name, 'pass' if ok else 'FAIL'))
print('%d/%d pass; add a case = add a row' % (len(cases) - failed, len(cases)))

title: Regression suites
description: Regression suites are the project's memory: every fixed bug gets a test that fails without the fix, so the bug can never silently return. The discipline is the test-first bugfix — reproduce, then fix, then keep the test. Suites grow monotonically; the maintenance is pruning obsolete tests and keeping runtime under the CI budget. A bug without a regression test will be reintroduced; it is only a matter of time.
mechanism: Bug -> reproducer test (fails) -> fix (passes) -> keep forever. Tag with the issue id. Runtime budget enforced in CI; slow tests quarantined, not deleted.
algo: O(suite) per run; the value compounds — each test is a bug that stays fixed.

title: Test smells
description: Test code rots too: mystery guests (hidden fixtures), eager tests (asserting everything), slow tests, flaky tests, and assertion roulette (many asserts, one failure message). Test smells make the suite untrusted — and an untrusted suite gets ignored, which is worse than no suite. The fixes are the same as production code: names, isolation, speed, determinism.
mechanism: Detect: runtime per test, flakiness rate, assert counts, fixture complexity. Fix: split eager tests, isolate with fakes, quarantine flaky ones with an owner and a deadline (fix or delete).
algo: O(suite) measurement; the fixes are refactoring.
demo:
import time

# assertion roulette: 5 asserts, one failure, no message saying which
def test_roulette():
    results = []
    results.append(('a', 1 == 1))
    results.append(('b', 2 == 2))
    results.append(('c', 3 == 4))  # fails: which one? the message won't say
    results.append(('d', 4 == 4))
    failed = [n for n, ok in results if not ok]
    return failed

print('failed assertions:', test_roulette(), '(roulette: split into named tests)')
print('smells: mystery guests, eager tests, slow, flaky, roulette')
print('an untrusted suite gets ignored: worse than no suite')

title: Flaky test detection
description: Flaky tests pass and fail without code changes — timing, ordering, randomness, shared state. Detection is statistical: run the suite N times (or track history) and flag tests with mixed results. The quarantine workflow: flaky test gets an owner and a deadline; it runs in a separate lane (not blocking merges) until fixed or deleted. There is no third option — a flaky test in the blocking suite poisons every PR.
mechanism: History tracking per test (pass/fail over runs); flakiness score = entropy of outcomes. Quarantine lane for the flaky; bisect to find the cause (usually: time, order, shared mutable state).
algo: O(runs * suite) detection; the fix is determinism (seed, isolate, fake time).
demo:
import random

# flaky: depends on wall-clock timing
def test_timing():
    import time
    t = time.perf_counter()
    time.sleep(0.001)
    return (time.perf_counter() - t) < 0.0005  # sometimes true, sometimes not

results = [test_timing() for _ in range(20)]
print('20 runs:', sum(results), 'pass /', 20 - sum(results), 'fail (SAME code)')
print('FLAKY: quarantine with owner + deadline; fix (fake the clock) or delete')
print('no third option: flaky tests in the blocking suite poison every PR')

title: Testing in CI
description: Tests only matter if they run: CI runs the suite on every PR, with sharding for speed, retries for flakes (limited, tracked), and required status checks. The architecture is pipeline stages — fast unit tests first (fail fast), then integration, then the slow suite — so developers get signal in minutes. Test selection (only affected tests) keeps big repos fast; the full suite runs nightly.
mechanism: Stages by speed; sharding by test count; affected-test selection from the dependency graph; SARIF/JUnit output for tracking. Budgets: PR signal in <10 min, full suite nightly.
algo: O(affected) per PR with selection; O(suite) nightly. Sharding is division, not magic.
demo:
# pipeline stages: fast first (fail fast), slow later; affected-only per PR
stages = [
    ('unit (fast)', 120, 'affected only'),
    ('integration', 40, 'affected only'),
    ('e2e (slow)', 15, 'nightly full'),
]
print('%-16s %6s %s' % ('stage', 'tests', 'scope'))
for name, n, scope in stages:
    print('%-16s %6d %s' % (name, n, scope))
print('PR signal in minutes: fail fast on unit, select affected, full suite nightly')

title: Benchmarking test generation
description: Test-generation techniques are benchmarked on real bugs: generate tests for the pre-fix code and measure which generated tests fail (catching the bug) — the honest metric. Benchmarks use mined bug-fix commits with their regression tests as ground truth. A generator that writes pretty tests catching nothing is decoration; one catching 30% of real bugs is a tool.
mechanism: Corpus: (buggy version, fixed version, human regression test). Generate tests on buggy; run on fixed; a good generated test fails on buggy and passes on fixed. Report the catch rate.
algo: O(corpus * (generate + run)). The metric is bug catch rate, not test count.
